[1] ICAO, Procedures for Air Navigation Services – Air Traffic Management[2] SKYbrary, Standard phraseology
1) The detector predicts that AC1 and AC2, flying head-on on the same route at FL300, lose separation at t = 112.5 s (scenario sample_conflict of the course). 2) The Executive Controller gives AC2 a climb to FL320; now they are 2000 ft apart, the Verification Officer finds no conflict and the clearance is written in standard phraseology. Separation minima from ICAO: 5 NM horizontal, 1000 ft vertical; a conflict exists only when both are broken at the same time. The system is offline: all inputs are files given at the start, and it ends with a Markdown report.

Each agent copies a real role in air traffic management, so its responsibility is clear and easy to justify. Scope: en-route conflict detection and resolution, as an area controller does. Out of scope: runway choice (approach control; our data has nodes but no runways) and live radar data.

Five properties from Lecture 21 and Wooldridge2  ·  also multi-agent (all cooperative) and known (rules fixed before the run)3
[1] MAS course, Lecture 2: Agent Architectures, URV 2026[2] Wooldridge, An Introduction to MultiAgent Systems, 2nd ed., 2009[3] Russell & Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 2020
Our agents do not see a real airspace: they see one scenario given as files (three required, three optional), and the system reads them, writes the report and stops. For a real ATC centre almost every answer would be the opposite. Accessible: all the information is in the input files from the start and every crew reads the same intermediate files; the only limit is that the weather snapshot is a forecast, but for the system it is the complete information. Deterministic (in the model): aircraft follow their plans, the wind of each hour is fixed and zones come from fixed thresholds, so the same scenario and the same manoeuvre always give the same trajectories and conflicts; that is why every calculation is a deterministic tool. The LLM can answer differently in each run, but that is a property of the agents, not of the environment. Non-episodic inside a run: moving one aircraft can create a new conflict or enter a zone, which is why we added Safety Validation; across runs it is episodic, nothing is kept. Static: nothing new arrives during a run; zone time windows are known from the start; flagging a conflict for a human controller does not stop the run. Discrete by design: waypoint graph, finite list of records, conflicts per segment, zone checks at fixed time steps and four manoeuvre types. From Russell & Norvig: multi-agent but fully cooperative (aircraft are not agents, they just follow their plans) and known (separation minima and thresholds fixed before the run).

How we decided: five design rules

1
New crew only for a new step
own input, output file and decision point: otherwise it is an agent
2
One detector
every conflict is found by the same deterministic tool
3
Numbers from tools, decisions from agents
the LLM never computes a separation1
4
Files as the interface
one Pydantic JSON per crew → each crew testable alone2
5
Static inputs
nothing is downloaded during a run → repeatable results
[1] ICAO, Procedures for Air Navigation Services – Air Traffic Management[2] URV, MAS Practical Work 2026–2027 (assignment)
We agreed on these rules in the forum before discussing any proposal; each member proposed ideas with a common template (idea, motivation, agents and tools, place in the flow). Every later decision applies one of them: new crew vs. new agent (rule 1), the shared detector (rule 2), deterministic tools (rule 3), intermediate files (rule 4) and no live data (rule 5).

[1] ICAO, Procedures for Air Navigation Services – ATM[2] Open-Meteo, Weather forecast API[3] EUROCONTROL, ERNIP Part 3 – Flexible Use of Airspace[4] SKYbrary, ATC ops in weather avoidance
Each scenario folder has the three files required by the assignment and three optional files we added. Required: the airspace graph (waypoints with latitude and longitude, airways with distance in NM), the aircraft (ID and cruise speed, plus an optional status with the special-handling indicator STS/HOSP or STS/MEDEVAC, or the emergency code 7700, from ICAO), and the flight plans (route, departure time, cruise altitude; the first and last waypoints are the airports). Optional: weather.json is real data from Open-Meteo, downloaded once by a script and saved in the scenario folder, so runs are repeatable; it covers the whole graph plus 20 NM, every level Tactical may assign (cruise level ± 4000 ft) and the maximum delay, so Safety Validation never needs new weather. restricted_zones.json follows the Flexible Use of Airspace idea: shape, flight-level band and active time windows. airport_constraints.json: closures, ground stops, reduced capacity, with affected movements and a time window. The thresholds that turn weather into hazard zones are kept in hazard_thresholds.yaml, each with its reference (CAPE for storms, 20 NM buffer, turbulence wind, icing temperatures). If an optional file is missing the crew writes an empty list. Invalid flight plans (unknown aircraft, node or airway) are rejected by FDA with the reason, not repaired, and listed in the report.

Why Airspace Constraints
  • Wind changes ETAs; storms are avoided by ~20 NM1
  • Storms, military zones, airport closures → one constraint-zone model2
  • Input data through:
→  airport_constraints.json
→  restricted_zones.json
→  weather.json
Why Safety Validation
  • A fix can create a new conflict
  • Tactical must not grade its own work3
  • Reuses the same detector (rule 2)
Other proposals and decisions
  • Agents, not crews (rule 1): Priority Officer, Airspace Manager, Radio Officer
  • Rejected: live weather download (not repeatable)
  • Future work: runway choice
[1] SKYbrary, ATC operations in weather avoidance scenarios[2] EUROCONTROL, ERNIP Part 3 – Flexible Use of Airspace, 2024[3] SKYbrary, Medium term conflict detection (MTCD)
Airspace Constraints started as a weather proposal: wind changes ground speed, so ETAs, so whether two aircraft meet; storms create areas to avoid (crews keep about 20 NM from a cumulonimbus). Restricted/military zones and airport constraints are not weather, but they are the same kind of object, so one crew turns every source into a constraint zone. It runs after Data Management, not in parallel with it, because it needs its output: the trajectories define the area, flight levels and time window the constraints must cover, and the first and last node of each route are the airports. It must finish before Surveillance because the detector needs the wind for correct ETAs and the zones to check the trajectories. Safety Validation replaces our first draft loop back to Surveillance: a manoeuvre can solve one conflict and create another, and Tactical should not grade its own work. Inside each crew the process is sequential, with independent tasks running asynchronously (AM in parallel with the weather agents; TP and FPO after FDA); what runs next is decided by deterministic Flow routers, not a manager LLM.

Phraseology
Short definitions (role, goal, task), as the assignment asks. All tools are deterministic: FileReadTool is built in, the other ten are custom BaseTools. ConflictDetectionTool wraps the course notebook detector and is shared by RC and VO. ManoeuvreSimulatorTool is a what-if tool so EC can test an idea before proposing it; VO still checks the final proposal. PhraseologyTool fills fixed templates because non-standard phraseology contributes to incidents. SUP reuses SeverityTool to judge each manoeuvre. Tactical has a single agent on purpose: one decision maker, checked by another crew. Future work: split conflicts into independent groups (connected components of the conflict graph) and run one Tactical crew per group in parallel, like ATC sectors.

Router 1 sends the flow to Tactical if 02_surveillance.json has at least one conflict (traffic or zone), otherwise straight to Reporting, as the assignment requires. Router 2 goes to Reporting if every manoeuvre is approved; if some are rejected and the counter is below two, it goes back to Tactical with the Supervisor's feedback, and only the rejected conflicts are solved again. The counter starts at 0 and counts how many times the flow went back to Tactical; if the conflict is still rejected when the counter is two (third attempt), the flow goes to Reporting and the conflict is flagged 'requires human controller' with the last manoeuvre and the reason. The counter lives in the Flow state, not in an agent, so no language model can skip the limit.

Properties, architectures and types as in the course [1, 2, 3]
[1] MAS course, Lecture 2: Agent Architectures, URV 2026[2] MAS course, Lecture 3: Agent Properties and Types, URV 2026[3] Wooldridge, An Introduction to MultiAgent Systems, 2nd ed., 2009
Three features of the design explain most of the table: the system runs once and stops; all calculations are done by deterministic tools; agents exchange information through files with a fixed Pydantic structure. Rows are grouped by crew. Most agents (FDA, TP, FPO, WDC, WHA, AM, RC, VO and RCO) have few properties because they apply a fixed procedure with a tool; EC and SUP have almost all of them because they handle the open part of the problem: how to solve each conflict. Flexibility = adaptive + proactive + social at the same time: only EC and SUP. FDA, CA and RO are partially flexible: FDA reports invalid plans instead of stopping, CA orders the conflicts when the criteria disagree, RO adapts the report to how the run ended. Reactivity: the environment is static, so we judged it on the information received from other agents; EC, VO and SUP get new plans or feedback on every iteration. Proactiveness: EC, SUP and CA fully (CA gives Tactical an order of work); RO partially (points out critical cases without being asked); FPO and WDC apply fixed rules, so they are not proactive. Social ability is partial for most: files work like a blackboard; only EC and SUP have a real two-way exchange. RCO's output is a directive speech act, but nobody answers it inside the system. Rationality: everyone, because numbers come from tools and every manoeuvre is checked. Reasoning: CA, EC, SUP fully, RO partially. Learning: only EC partially (uses SUP feedback within a run). Autonomy limited by design: SUP must approve, the retry counter lives in the Flow. No temporal continuity or mobility: one-shot run on one machine. Architectures and types follow the report's Table 8: CA is hybrid but an information agent, VO is reactive and informational, RO is hybrid and an interface agent.
